domain_reasoning: Apart from talking, the time goes into entering the order in the billing or account system.
length_reasoning: A simple address change takes a couple of minutes; a new contract or a discontinuance with final-bill questions takes around ten to fifteen.
review_reasoning: A reviewer listens to the contact, mostly at higher speed, and checks the submitted order against what the customer asked for; longer contracts need fields checked one by one.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong order causes a wrong bill, a missed move or a wrongly stopped service, usually corrected after a complaint; a wrong contract term can be costly.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's order screens, product rules and required fields, learned over a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The time goes into opening billing, usage and case records and checking outside information such as weather, then writing the finding.
length_reasoning: A simple bill complaint is checked against usage and rates in about fifteen minutes; a disputed multi-month case with outside data takes an hour or more.
review_reasoning: A supervisor reads the finding and checks it against the key records; a typical case needs the usage and rate evidence reopened; a complex case needs the chain of evidence followed.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong finding leads to a wrongly refused or wrongly granted adjustment, reaching the customer and reversible with rework or a complaint.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's billing systems, tariffs, adjustment policy and case history, picked up over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The output is written test cases and scripts, read from requirements, mostly in a test management tool or documents; the time is spent reading and writing text rather than code.
length_reasoning: A small feature needs a handful of cases in under an hour; a complex feature with many paths and scripted steps takes most of a day.
review_reasoning: A test lead reads the requirements, then reads the cases for coverage and clarity; larger sets need more careful coverage checking.
stakes_reasoning: Gaps in cases let defects through to later testing or release, mostly caught later and fixed, with some customer-visible bugs.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the product and its behaviour and the team's test conventions, built over weeks to months.

domain_reasoning: A test plan is a document written from requirements and scope.
length_reasoning: A plan for a small change is a short document in a couple of hours; a plan for a full release takes a couple of days.
review_reasoning: A test lead reads the plan against scope and risks; a release plan needs the scope, risks and schedule examined carefully.
stakes_reasoning: A flawed plan misses areas or underestimates effort, found later and costing rework or schedule, rarely a direct loss.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the product, release process, environments and team, built over months.

domain_reasoning: Most of the time goes into operating the application under test and test tools, running steps and logging results and defects.
length_reasoning: A small change is tested in under an hour; a larger change with regression runs and several defects takes a day or more.
review_reasoning: A release manager reads the results and defects and spot-checks some executions; larger cycles need more re-checking of failures and coverage.
stakes_reasoning: A wrongly signed-off change can reach production and cause an outage or customer-facing failure.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the system, test environment and what the change is meant to do, built over months.

domain_reasoning: The worker enters a summary and codes in the CRM or case system, and some typing of notes.
length_reasoning: A routine contact needs a code and a couple of lines in a minute or two; a complex contact needs a longer summary and several actions logged.
review_reasoning: A reviewer reads the record and compares it with the call recording or account history; longer contacts need more time to check against the recording.
stakes_reasoning: A poor record misleads later agents or reporting and is usually fixed when noticed, with occasional rework or disputes.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's disposition codes and record conventions, learned in a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The worker opens the account or order system and compares the record with the expected change.
length_reasoning: A simple check is a lookup and close in a few minutes; a case with a discrepancy needs more digging and reopening.
review_reasoning: A supervisor opens the case and the account record and confirms the change; a discrepancy case needs the history read.
stakes_reasoning: A missed failed change leaves the customer's problem unresolved, noticed on the next bill or contact and fixed with rework.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's systems and case conventions, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The work is editing and running test script code, then handling review and the pipeline.
length_reasoning: A small locator or step fix takes under an hour; a larger product change that breaks many scripts takes a day.
review_reasoning: A code reviewer reads the diff and the pipeline result; larger changes need the scripts and changed product behaviour compared.
stakes_reasoning: A bad script update can hide regressions or produce false failures, usually caught in the pipeline or later runs.
context_reasoning: Needs the test framework, repository conventions and product behaviour, learned over weeks to months.

domain_reasoning: Most of the time goes into operating imaging tools, admin consoles and installers rather than writing text or code.
length_reasoning: A standard image-based setup takes about an hour of active work; one with special software or account problems takes several.
review_reasoning: An IT supervisor or colleague checks the machine against the setup checklist, logging in and verifying software and accounts.
stakes_reasoning: A missed configuration shows up when the employee starts and is fixed with a short support visit; security settings missed would matter more.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's images, software list, accounts and policies, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The worker reads code or the running program against written standards and writes up deviations and recommendations.
length_reasoning: A small program takes an hour or so to check against a checklist; a large build with many deviations takes most of a day.
review_reasoning: A QA lead reads the report and verifies a sample of deviations against the standard and the program; larger reports need more verification.
stakes_reasoning: Missed deviations are found later in audits or review and fixed; occasionally a compliance gap matters.
context_reasoning: Needs the applicable standards and the team's code base and conventions, learned over weeks to months.

domain_reasoning: The time goes into reading logs, configuration files and code to trace the failure.
length_reasoning: Obvious failures are traced in minutes; obscure ones take a couple of hours of log reading and reproducing.
review_reasoning: A developer reads the diagnosis and checks the cited log lines or code; harder cases need the reasoning followed through.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong diagnosis sends developers the wrong way and costs time, caught when the fix fails.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the system architecture, logs and past behaviour, built over months.

domain_reasoning: The worker fills in the vendor's web portal or form, looks up warranty information and updates the ticket.
length_reasoning: A simple RMA with known details takes a quarter of an hour; a complex case with logs and serials to gather takes an hour.
review_reasoning: A supervisor opens the ticket and vendor case and checks details and warranty info; complex cases need attachments read.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong referral delays the repair or loses warranty coverage; the user is without equipment for longer, but it can be corrected.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's vendors, contracts, asset records and warranty status, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: Most time goes into setting up environments, running tests across configurations and filing issues in tools.
length_reasoning: A small matrix takes a few hours; a large matrix of operating systems, browsers and devices takes more than a day of active work.
review_reasoning: A QA lead reads the results matrix, checks filed issues and re-runs a sample; larger matrices need more spot checks.
stakes_reasoning: Missed incompatibilities reach customers with specific setups and cause support issues and fixes.
context_reasoning: Needs the product, supported configurations and test lab, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The work is configuring fields, workflows and permissions in a tracker tool.
length_reasoning: Using a standard template takes a few hours; a custom workflow with migration of existing defects takes a couple of days.
review_reasoning: A QA manager walks through the configuration, tries a workflow and checks the fields; custom setups need more testing.
stakes_reasoning: Poor configuration causes rework and data cleaning for the team but can be changed.
context_reasoning: Needs the team's defect process, terminology and tooling, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The output is a report built from workflow analysis, cost comparisons and writing, mostly reading and writing documents.
length_reasoning: A narrow study takes a couple of days; a broad study with interviews, space design and costing takes weeks of active work.
review_reasoning: An IT manager reads the report, checks the figures and recommendation; larger studies need the assumptions and sources examined.
stakes_reasoning: A flawed study leads management to a poor investment or a failed rollout, costly and hard to reverse.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the organisation's workflows, people, budgets and systems, built over months.

domain_reasoning: The worker writes a guide, taking screenshots and text, mostly document writing.
length_reasoning: A short how-to takes an hour or two; a full guide with screenshots and testing takes a day.
review_reasoning: A supervisor reads the guide and follows the steps on the system to check they work; longer guides take longer to follow.
stakes_reasoning: Wrong steps mislead users who then ask for help or make mistakes, reversible with rework.
context_reasoning: Needs the organisation's systems and user needs, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The worker reads the ticket, operates the product and logs to try to reproduce, and files findings in tools.
length_reasoning: Easy reproductions take a short while; problems tied to a customer's setup or data take half a day.
review_reasoning: A developer or support reads the findings and may re-run the reproduction steps; harder cases need more checking.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong finding sends the customer wrong advice or hides a real defect; it reaches the customer and is reversible.
context_reasoning: Needs the product's internals, customer configurations and history, built over months.
